answer.label: Not Mark Twain — a 1987 country song lyric
answer.sourceLine: The line is a reworded scrap of the chorus of “Come from the Heart,” written in 1987 by Susanna Clark and Richard Leigh and first recorded by Don Williams that year. Quote Investigator ↗ states flatly that there is no substantive support for ascribing it to Mark Twain, and credits the lyric to Clark and Leigh.
answer.confidenceText: Traced by Quote Investigator to a 1987 song lyric; nothing connects it to Mark Twain.

source.trailTitle: How a lyric became a Twain quote
trail: 1987 — the song is written. Susanna Clark and Richard Leigh compose “Come from the Heart”; its chorus contains the dancing and loving lines that later float free. Quote Investigator credits the lyric to Clark and Leigh ↗.
1987–1989 — it reaches a mass audience. Don Williams records it first, on Traces; Kathy Mattea’s version becomes a number-one country single in 1989 ↗.
2001–2004 — the names arrive. A Chapel Hill columnist credits William Purkey in 2001; by 2004 a Charlotte newspaper has handed the “heaven on earth” version to Mark Twain, per Quote Investigator ↗.
The writer objects. Richard Leigh tells Songfacts that people cannot find an earlier printed or recorded version because “they don’t exist” ↗.
source.excerptNote: Shown here is the circulating internet wording, not the song. The underlying chorus of “Come from the Heart” — which pairs singing as though you don’t need the money with dancing unobserved and loving without fear of hurt — is copyrighted lyric, so we describe rather than reproduce it. The popular sentence reorders and rewrites those lines.

source.rightsNote: The words originate in “Come from the Heart,” a song written in 1987 — far too recent for the public domain in the United States, where works first published in 1931 or later remain protected. The reworded sentence that circulates online has no identified author of its own; treat the underlying lyric as fully in copyright and do not assume the popular paraphrase is free to reuse.

author.name: Susanna Clark & Richard Leigh
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: Susanna Clark (1939–2012) & Richard Leigh (b. 1951) · Nashville songwriters
author.bio: Susanna Clark was a Texas-born songwriter and painter who moved to Nashville in 1971 and was married to singer-songwriter Guy Clark; her songs include “I’ll Be Your San Antone Rose.” Richard Leigh, born in Washington, D.C. in 1951, wrote “Don’t It Make My Brown Eyes Blue” for Crystal Gayle and was inducted into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame in 1994. Together they wrote “Come from the Heart” in 1987 — and Leigh has spent years insisting, correctly, that the famous lines are theirs and not some anonymous piece of folk wisdom.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: The saying circulates in a dozen shuffled forms, usually padded with extra lines about singing and living like it’s heaven on earth. Three names collect most of the credit, and none of them earned it.

items.why: Quote Investigator reports that by 2004 the “heaven on earth” version had been reassigned to Twain in a Charlotte newspaper quote collection, and states there is no substantive support for the ascription ↗. Twain died in 1910, decades before the lyric was written.
Paige’s genuine aphorisms attract company. Quote Investigator groups him with Twain as having no substantive support ↗ for the saying.

A 2001 Chapel Hill Herald column credited the “heaven on earth” version to the author and speaker William Purkey; Yale Book of Quotations editor Fred Shapiro later reported that he had corresponded with Purkey, who was unable to supply reliable documentation ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The credit belongs to Susanna Clark and Richard Leigh, who wrote “Come from the Heart” in 1987 — a conclusion reached by Quote Investigator ↗ and confirmed by Leigh himself ↗.

context.heading: Why a country chorus became internet Twain
lead: The lyric came out of Nashville in 1987, went to No. 1 on the country chart in Kathy Mattea’s 1989 recording, and then slipped its moorings. Stripped of its melody, reshuffled and padded with extra clauses about singing and heaven on earth, it started circulating as anonymous wisdom — and anonymous wisdom, on the internet, eventually gets a famous name stapled to it.

Mark Twain is the default recipient. He is quotable, long dead, and out of copyright in the popular imagination, which makes him a magnet for feel-good lines he never wrote. The tell here is chronology: Twain died in 1910, and the earliest documentation Quote Investigator finds for this saying is the 1987 song.
detailsBody: Richard Leigh has pushed back publicly. Asked why people keep hunting for an older printed source, he told Songfacts that they can’t find one because, in his words, “they don’t exist” — adding that people seem disappointed the lines came from ordinary working songwriters.
Yale Book of Quotations editor Fred Shapiro looked into the rival claim for educator William W. Purkey and reported, per Quote Investigator, that Purkey was unable to supply reliable documentation.
context.pull: Twain died in 1910. The line was written in 1987.
